title: Review: Thermodynamics; Current and circuits
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: B.5#c24 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; B.5#c18 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; B.5#c23 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; B.5.15#xt1 term and clue written for the game. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Potentiometer (potential divider)
items.clue: A resistor with a sliding contact.

items.label: Light-dependent resistor (LDR)
items.clue: A semiconductor component that conducts better as illumination increases.

items.label: Thermistor
items.clue: NTC component whose opposition to current falls as its temperature rises.

questions.stem: A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?

options.text: Free electrons drift slowly, in the opposite direction to the conventional current.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, in the same direction as the conventional current.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.

questions.stem: A battery of emf 9.0 V, a switch and a lamp are connected in series. The switch is open. An ideal voltmeter is connected first across the switch and then across the lamp. What are the two readings?

options.text: Across both the switch and the lamp 0 V
Across the switch 9.0 V; across the lamp 0 V
Across the switch 4.5 V; across the lamp 4.5 V
Across each of the switch and lamp 9.0 V

questions.explanation: With the switch open there is no current, so the pd across the lamp is IR = 0 and there is no pd across any internal resistance. By the loop rule the pds must add up to the emf, so the full 9.0 V appears across the gap in the switch: work would be done on a charge moved across it, even though none flows.

questions.stem: A copper wire and a solution of sodium chloride form part of the same series circuit, and a steady current flows in both. What are the charge carriers in the wire and in the solution?

options.text: Free electrons in the wire and also in the solution, because a current is a flow of electrons in any conductor.
Protons in the wire, moving from the positive terminal to the negative; positive and negative ions in the solution.
Charge released by the cell, which flows out through the wire, on through the solution and back to the cell.
Free electrons in the wire; in the solution, positive ions and negative ions that move through it in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A constant pd is applied across a metal wire, so an electric field acts on the free electrons. Why do the electrons drift along the wire at a constant average velocity rather than accelerating continuously?

options.text: Friction between the electrons and the inner surface of the wire balances the force from the field.
They gain speed between collisions with the lattice ions but lose it again at each collision.
Collisions with the other electrons crowding through the wire keep them all moving at one speed.
They already travel at almost the speed of light, so the field cannot make them go any faster.

questions.stem: The pd across and the current in four components are measured. W: 9.0 V and 3.0 A. X: 2.0 V and 4.0 A. Y: 3.0 V and 0.60 A. Z: 0.80 V and 0.20 A. Which component has the greatest resistance?

options.text: W
Y
X
Z

questions.explanation: Resistance is the ratio R = V/I. Component Y has 3.0 V / 0.60 A = 5.0 Ω, larger than W (3.0 Ω), X (0.50 Ω) and Z (4.0 Ω). Neither the largest pd nor the smallest current on its own identifies the largest resistance.

questions.stem: Wire X has resistance R and is made of a material of resistivity ρ. Wire Y is made of the same material at the same temperature, but it is twice as long as X and has twice the diameter of X. What are the resistance and the resistivity of wire Y?

options.text: resistance R, resistivity ρ
resistance R/2, resistivity ρ/2
resistance 8R, resistivity ρ
resistance R/2, resistivity ρ

questions.explanation: R = ρL/A. Doubling the length doubles R; doubling the diameter quadruples the area, which divides R by 4. So R_Y = R × 2/4 = R/2. Resistivity is a property of the material at a given temperature, so it is unchanged: ρ.

questions.stem: A student measures the resistance of a length of metal wire as 5.0 Ω, using a pd of 1.0 V. The student claims that, by Ohm's law, the current in the wire will be 2.4 A when the pd is increased to 12 V. Which statement about this claim is correct?

options.text: It holds only if the wire is at the same temperature at 12 V as it was at 1.0 V.
It holds, because 5.0 Ω is a fixed property of this wire whatever pd is applied to it.
It holds only if the wire is a metal, because every metal conductor obeys Ohm's law.
It fails, because the resistance rises to 60 Ω, in proportion to the pd across the wire.

questions.stem: As the pd across a filament lamp is increased, the ratio V/I for the lamp increases. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: More of the current is used up in the filament at higher pd, so less passes through it.
The filament heats up; its ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often.
The filament expands as it heats up, and its extra length increases its resistance.
At higher current the electrons crowd together and collide with one another more.

questions.explanation: The current heats the filament (the heating effect of a current). At a higher temperature the lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude, electron–ion collisions become more frequent, and the resistance V/I increases.

questions.stem: A 4.0 Ω resistor and an 8.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a dc supply. Which resistor dissipates more power, and why?

options.text: The 8.0 Ω resistor dissipates twice as much, since P = I²R and its resistance is larger.
The 4.0 Ω resistor dissipates twice as much, since both have the same pd and P = V²/R.
Both dissipate the same power, since each has the same pd and the current splits equally.
The 8.0 Ω resistor dissipates twice as much, since it takes the larger share of the pd.

questions.stem: Two identical filament lamps P and Q are connected in series with a cell of negligible internal resistance, in the order: positive terminal, lamp P, lamp Q, negative terminal. How do the brightnesses of the lamps compare?

options.text: They are equally bright, and each is as bright as a single lamp on the cell.
P is brighter, since some of the current is used up in P before it reaches Q.
Q is brighter, as the electrons leave the negative terminal and so reach Q first.
They are equally bright, and each is dimmer than a single lamp on the cell.

questions.explanation: In series the current is the same in both lamps (I = I₁ = I₂), and identical lamps carrying the same current have the same pd and the same power, so they are equally bright. The two lamps share the supply pd, so each has less pd and less current than one lamp alone, and each is dimmer.

questions.stem: A potentiometer has a uniform resistance track connected across a 9.0 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected between one end of the track and the sliding contact, which is one third of the way along the track from that end. What does the voltmeter read?
questions.explanation: The two parts of the track are in series and carry the same current, so the pd divides in proportion to resistance. The part between the end and the slider has one third of the track's resistance, so its pd is 9.0 × 1/3 = 3.0 V.

questions.stem: A filament lamp A is connected across a cell of negligible internal resistance. An identical lamp B is then connected in parallel with A. What happens to the brightness of A and to the current from the cell?

options.text: A becomes dimmer, since the cell's current is now shared between two lamps.
A becomes dimmer, since the pd across A is now shared with lamp B.
A is unchanged in brightness, and the current from the cell doubles.
A is unchanged, and so is the cell current, as B's branch is separate from A's.

questions.explanation: A and B are both connected directly across the cell, so each has the full emf across it (V = V₁ = V₂). A's pd, current and power are unchanged. The cell now supplies both branches, so the total current is I = I₁ + I₂, twice the original.

questions.stem: The first law of thermodynamics, Q = ΔU + W, is applied to a closed system using Clausius' sign convention. Which statement about the law is correct?

options.text: It applies to a system that no energy can enter or leave, because a closed system is sealed off from its surroundings.
Q is the thermal energy that the system contains, and it forms one part of the system's total internal energy U.
Q and W are properties of the state of the system, as U is, so each depends only on the initial and final states.
It is conservation of energy: the thermal energy supplied equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done by the system.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is taken from state X to state Y. On a P–V diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis) the process is a straight line from X (2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) to Y (6.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa), where each state is given as (volume, pressure). What is the work W, as it appears in Q = ΔU + W, for this process?
questions.explanation: The pressure is not constant, so W is the area under the straight-line path, a trapezium: W = ½(1.0 × 10⁵ + 3.0 × 10⁵) Pa × 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 800 J. It is positive because the gas expands.

questions.stem: Two identical samples, X and Y, each contain the same amount of helium, a monatomic ideal gas, at 300 K. X is heated at constant volume and Y is heated at constant pressure, and both finish at 350 K. Which comparison of the two processes is correct?

options.text: ΔU is greater for Y, as more thermal energy must be supplied to Y than to X.
Y has the smaller ΔU, since it loses some of its energy as work as it expands.
ΔU is greater for Y, since its atoms move further apart and gain potential energy.
ΔU is the same for both, but more thermal energy must be supplied to Y than to X.

questions.explanation: ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT depends only on the temperature change, which is the same for both. Y expands and does work W = nRΔT, so it needs Q = ΔU + W, more than X, for which W = 0 and Q = ΔU.

questions.stem: Four identical fair coins are tossed. Each particular sequence of heads (H) and tails (T), such as HTHT, is a microstate, and all microstates are equally probable. The macrostate is the total number of heads. What is the probability of the macrostate 'two heads'?
questions.explanation: There are 2⁴ = 16 equally probable microstates. Six of them have exactly two heads: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH and TTHH. P = 6/16 = 37.5%.

questions.stem: An inventor claims to have built a device that, operating in a cycle, extracts 1000 J of thermal energy from seawater at 290 K in each cycle and delivers 1000 J of work, with no other effect. Which judgement of this claim is correct?

options.text: Impossible: although it conserves energy, it breaks the Kelvin form of the second law.
Possible: the work output equals the thermal energy input, so no law of physics is broken.
Impossible: seawater at 290 K is cold, so it contains no thermal energy to extract.
Possible, but only if all friction and heat leaks in the device are removed.

questions.stem: A hot copper block and a cold copper block are placed in contact inside a sealed, perfectly insulated box, so that together they form an isolated system. They reach a common temperature. Which statement about entropy is correct?

options.text: The total entropy is unchanged, because the entropy lost by the hot block is gained by the cold block.
The total entropy increases, because heat flow across a temperature difference is irreversible.
The entropy of each block increases, because thermal energy flows between the two blocks.
The total entropy increases, because some of the energy is destroyed as the blocks come to equilibrium.
